## Manual of Regular Conduct for Women

Generally, one must learn the family traditions of a wise mother and harmonize the heart so that one’s conduct is upright. This is to be held most precious; one must combine this with a mind that values virtue. A person’s <term>haengsil</term> <gloss>conduct</gloss> is the very beginning of determining what kind of person they are. 

Within the home, a woman must practice <term>hyo</term> <gloss>filial piety</gloss> toward her parents and serve them to maintain the virtue of filial duty. Furthermore, she must go forth to serve the ruler with <term>chung</term> <gloss>loyalty</gloss>, fulfilling her duties with respect. If one does not strive to be wise in serving elders, or if one does not serve them with the "Good Way" without ceasing, then they fail. 

One should restore their daily conduct and observe their friends. In the future, follow the path of <term>hyo</term> <gloss>filial piety</gloss> and keep the duties of a woman. Do not follow the desire to ignore filial piety, but rather remove the vessel of helping others <note>likely a metaphor for selfish interference</note>. Remove such thoughts and do not proceed with them; instead, keep the <term>nyeoja-ui do</term> <gloss>the Way of Women</gloss>. Purify the path that has become rough and serve your parents with all your filial heart.

### Ministers Zheng and He Serve the Zhou as Directors of Education; Their Success Leads the People to Compose the "Black Robes" Poem

Zheng Shengchen and He Ergong <note>two legendary virtuous officials</note> successively served as the <term>Zhou Sitiao</term> <gloss>Minister of Education during the Zhou Dynasty</gloss>. They performed their duties with such excellence that the people of Zhou loved them and composed the poem <term>Ziyi</term> <gloss>Black Robes</gloss> in their honor.

The noble robes are worn at the foundation of the state; with great effort, they follow the path of ancestral narration. My garments are new. Through respectful ritual and diligent service to the King, they wear the silk sashes and belts, attending the gatherings of chariots and horses.
Like jade soaring to inherit a title, the poets signal this with their stanzas. The people submit to their virtue. Respectfully positioned as the screens of the feudal states, they manifest their achievements in all directions, focusing on the defense of the realm.

We reflect on how your Excellency’s family has inherited the tradition of jade and silk <note>symbols of high office and refinement</note>. The noble sons possess the beauty of generational continuity, with a sincerity that mends the <term>fufu</term> <gloss>sacrificial robes embroidered with ax patterns</gloss>. Following the words of the great officers who lived simply, they nearly became the "horse and fur" <note>symbolizing humble but sturdy support</note> of the royal house.
Their excellent virtue is fully expressed in their garments. Their dignified presence is a model for my investigation; their appearance should be carefully observed. People from all directions still follow these regulations, as the common people have long relied upon them.

Two generations have held office with true reverence. The decree follows these chapters, clearly showing our admiration for this era of prosperity. How beautiful is the education provided at court! The officials of the people are excellent, but their focus is on the diligent virtue represented by their service robes.
Why did the poets use objects to praise this excellence? It was to show a sincerity that does not grow weary, following the orderly succession of the <term>Yi</term> <gloss>Book of Changes</gloss> for auspiciousness. Like the Duke of Zhou assisting the King, they are as clear and strong as the "lamented robes" <note>referring to the concern for the state even in fine dress</note>.

Their goodness was great indeed during that time. The "Black Robes" poem was revised four times because of the love the people felt, a love they could not forget. Their meritorious deeds were great both before and after, leading to prayers for the excellence of their service garments.
There is a collection of poems that adorns their legacy. The children are brilliant and have the sincerity to support and aid; their songs reflect their thoughts. Their admiration reaches a point where it bursts forth in song, truly coming from an unwavering heart.

Only these songs of the people bring such abundant praise. Like the "Royal Airs" <note>a section of the Classic of Poetry</note> following the standard of the garments, we truly look up to the magnificent achievements of successive generations.
This proves the merit and virtue of our rulers. Like the common people who were once lost but now wear red garments <note>symbolizing status and protection</note>, we see the collective sentiment of those who admire this virtue.

# Gao Hao and Others of the Ming Dynasty Express Gratitude for the Instruction Regarding Their Home in Yunnan and the Gift of Summer Clothing

Today, as long-term guests in a distant land, we receive these clothes and look upon ourselves with pity. We express our thoughts through this memorial. From my lowly position in the desolate south, I look back toward the brickwork of <term>Bian</term> <gloss>Kaifeng</gloss> and the ten-thousand-mile journey to <term>Chang’an</term> <gloss>the capital</gloss>. We distant people receive this gift; how could we not walk with our heads held high? This was my initial ambition in my studies, yet for ten years I have lived as a traveler.

Knowing that my home in <term>Yunzhou</term> <gloss>Yunnan</gloss> is far away, the roads are said to be long. I feared the journey would be arduous for my family. At the edge of the sky, the road is difficult. As a traveler, I am always cut by the journey. These clothes had not yet been granted, and I sighed, feeling that good fortune was not shared between us. Through the cold of winter and the heat of summer, a warm robe and a traveler’s book were my companions as I walked under the moon. Successive assignments kept me from rest, and as a scholar, I rested only when others did.

If I were to lose what was before me, it would be the same. The evidence of my service is clear, though many do not listen. My worries as a traveler are overflowing; they invade me constantly. My dwelling has changed and is often in peril. From within, these clothes were sent from afar for the summer heat. They are precious ornaments, and I feared I would never wear them. Therefore, I preserve them to change my appearance; I, a lowly servant, must now dress as a scholar with a proper cap.

Why this formal document? The laws of spring and the passing days remind me of my distant home in the south. Without a home, I am merely a guest, relying on letters. As a guest on the road, spring arrives, and I receive the teacher's letters. Now, the gift of summer clothes has descended from the heavens. They are light garments granted by grace. For a guest of the palace, summer clothes are needed. Suddenly, I feel the need to wear them, moved by emotion.

The blessing of these summer clothes is profound. Without them, how could I handle the summer heat? It is not that I have no achievements or fame to my name, but I am bothered by the distance. I rely on this gift from afar. Traveling light, I reach the source of blessings. Having received these clothes today, I am filled with joy. The common customs are usually shameful, but this summer, the time is filled with brilliance.

The journey is supported, my injuries are healed by this grace. I envy myself, for although my strength is partial and I am but one person, I follow the excellence of these clothes. The spirit is restored, though I was thin and lowly before.
